title: Not All Teachers' Standards Are Equal: Why Priority Matters More Than Parity
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Dario Emanuele argues against treating every clause of the UK's Teachers' Standards as an equally urgent priority every minute of the day, calling that stance mathematically and mentally impossible to sustain. He proposes a strict three-tier hierarchy - behaviour management, then classroom routines, then accessible instruction - built on the premise that each tier is a precondition for the next, so collapse at a lower tier forces an immediate return to it rather than pressing on. He illustrates the framework with a personal account of a 'Perfect Storm' class combining high behavioural need, severe skill gaps, and group-protective defiance, describing how weeks spent purely on behaviour and routines in September made atomised, low-stakes instruction possible from week three onward. The piece leans heavily on named authorities in the UK evidence-informed teaching scene - Peps McCrea, Adam Boxer, Ollie Lovell, and Kris Boulton's atomisation framework - to ground the hierarchy in existing classroom-management and cognitive-load literature. Its central move is reframing teacher burnout not as an effort problem but as a sequencing problem: standards collapse into an unsustainable flat list unless a teacher imposes priority and drops back down the ladder whenever a lower rung slips.
points: Reframes the Teachers' Standards from a flat checklist into a dependency chain, arguing that treating every standard as equally urgent in every moment is the direct mechanical cause of teacher burnout, not merely a symptom of a hard job.
Names behaviour as the literal curriculum for an unmanaged class - explicit teaching of expectations, modeled and checked like any academic content, must precede any attempt at subject instruction.

Frames the September routine-rehearsal slowdown as a compounding investment rather than lost pace: automating entry, equipment, and transition routines by week four frees cognitive capacity that direct instruction can't otherwise access.

Uses atomisation - breaking a skill into its smallest teachable components - as the mechanism that makes complex content accessible once behaviour and routines are secure, directly tying cognitive-load reduction to classroom-management sequencing.

Demonstrates the hierarchy's real-world payoff through a 'Perfect Storm' class case study, where deliberately sacrificing curriculum coverage in weeks one and two produced measurable academic progress from week three onward, rather than daily friction and zero progress.
quotes: Your exquisite slide decks, your carefully crafted retrieval tasks, your atomised explanations, and your brilliant I Do, We Do, You Do scripts mean absolutely zero if the classroom is not silent, seated, and listening when direct instruction occurs.
Poor behaviour is a lead weight on school improvement, and there is little point focusing on anything else until it is fixed.

If a class does not know how to behave, then behaviour is your curriculum. As Ollie Lovell highlights in his Classroom Management Handbook, when behaviour breaks down, you must teach it explicitly as a subject.

holding back on the curriculum pace in September to rehearse entering the room silently, getting equipment out in 30 seconds, or executing a clean warm call routine feels counterintuitive. But this initial time investment pays massive dividends
Atomisation is the practice of breaking down a complex cognitive skill or concept into its absolute most fundamental constituent parts, both explicit and implicit, and teaching them systematically.

A Perfect Storm class is one where a rare, adverse combination of factors makes standard teaching nearly impossible: high behavioral or SEN needs, severe prior skill gaps, and the gang attitude, a tightly-knit group of peers who protect each other and collectively resist classroom expectations, turning individual off-task behaviour into a group event.

Did I cover as many textbook pages as the high-attaining set? No. But by adhering to the priority chain, the chaos vanished, learning actually happened, and every single student made measurable academic progress.
Organise your room by priorities. Get the behaviour silent and secure. Rehearse your routines until they are seamless. Atomise your content so every child can succeed.
